controversies.title: State Comptroller Audit: City Sidestepped $15,000 Sick Leave Payout Cap
controversies.entityInvolved: City of Clifton Administration & Union Contracts
controversies.summary: The New Jersey Office of the State Comptroller (OSC) investigated municipal sick leave payouts and explicitly cited Clifton for non-compliance with state reform laws.
controversies.investigationDetails: Under New Jersey law (P.L. 2010, c. 3), sick leave payouts for public employees hired after May 2010 must be capped at $15,000 and paid only upon formal retirement. The State Comptroller found that five out of six of Clifton's union contracts failed to implement the mandatory $15,000 cap, with provisions allowing up to 260 accrued sick days to be paid out as terminal leave or lump-sum exit payments. For a senior police officer or fire captain earning $140,000+, 260 days can equal over $100,000 in payouts for a single retiree.
controversies.taxpayerImpact: Hundreds of thousands of taxpayer dollars paid in terminal leave bonuses rather than capped at the state statutory limit.
controversies.status: Active finding; OSC recommends mandatory contract renegotiation and compliance audits.

controversies.title: PILOT Abatements Starve the Board of Education, Burden Homeowners
controversies.entityInvolved: City Council vs Clifton Board of Education vs Taxpayers
controversies.summary: Commercial real estate and multi-family apartment developments in Clifton have received long-term Payments In Lieu of Taxes (PILOT) agreements.
controversies.investigationDetails: Under NJ PILOT statutes, payments made by developers bypass the normal property tax formula. Instead of ~48% going to schools, 95% of PILOT funds go directly into City Hall's municipal general fund, 5% goes to Passaic County, and 0% goes to the Clifton Board of Education! When new residential complexes bring additional students into Clifton schools without contributing to the school tax levy, the Clifton BOE's expenses rise while existing single-family residential homeowners absorb higher school taxes.
controversies.taxpayerImpact: Directly explains why homeowners feel they bear an unfair burden of school taxes while large commercial redevelopments contribute zero to the school levy.
controversies.status: Ongoing council debate; subject of public protests and board of education pushback.

controversies.title: City Council Censure & Local Finance Board Referral
controversies.entityInvolved: Clifton City Council & Councilwoman Mary Sadrakula
controversies.summary: City Council approved a formal resolution of censure against Councilwoman Mary Sadrakula regarding workplace conduct and allegations of Open Public Meetings Act (OPMA) violations.
controversies.investigationDetails: The resolution directed that the matter be referred to the Local Finance Board (which enforces the Local Government Ethics Law) and relevant authorities to review interactions with city staff and municipal attorneys. The dispute exposed intense interpersonal friction inside City Hall and ongoing disputes over legal representation expenses.
controversies.taxpayerImpact: Thousands in municipal attorney legal billings spent on internal council litigation, censures, and external legal counsel opinions.
controversies.status: Formally passed resolution; ongoing friction in council deliberations.

controversies.title: School Board Ethics Filings & Consent Orders
controversies.summary: Multiple ethics complaints have been adjudicated by the New Jersey School Ethics Commission (SEC) involving Clifton Board of Education members.
controversies.investigationDetails: Past filings involved allegations of unauthorized public commentary outside board authority and conflicts surrounding district functions (e.g. Project Graduation, foreign policy declarations). While several counts were dismissed, certain matters resulted in SEC Consent Orders and formal admonishments reminding board trustees that individual members hold no individual administrative authority under N.J.S.A. 18A:12-24.1.
controversies.taxpayerImpact: District board attorney billing rates (often $175 - $225/hour) utilized to respond to and manage ethics commission inquiries.
controversies.status: Adjudicated with formal commission guidance on file.

controversies.title: Sudden City Manager Departure & Buyout Controversy
controversies.entityInvolved: Former City Manager Nick Villano & City Council
controversies.summary: After 15+ years heading city government, City Manager Nick Villano resigned abruptly effective April 1, 2025 amid intense friction with council members.
controversies.investigationDetails: The departure triggered confidential executive session discussions, legal notices, and public disputes over accumulated sick/vacation leave payouts and severance terms. Interim City Manager Gary DeMarzo was appointed while the city initiated search procedures, causing administrative instability across departments.
controversies.taxpayerImpact: Significant terminal payout packages and interim management restructuring costs.
controversies.status: Interim management active as of late 2026.

controversies.category: Secondary Employment & Traffic Detail Fund Oversight
controversies.title: Off-Duty Police Details & Outside Commercial Oversight
controversies.summary: Utility and road construction companies (e.g. PSE&G, telecom, paving) hire off-duty Clifton police officers for private traffic control details at premium rates.
controversies.investigationDetails: While contractors pay the bill (hourly officer pay plus a municipal administrative fee), citizen watchdogs and state audits have scrutinized outside employment arrangements to verify that officers are not working excessive consecutive hours (fatigue risks), that administrative overhead fees collected by the city fully cover cruiser fuel/wear, and that officers declare outside security firms properly.
controversies.taxpayerImpact: Cruiser vehicle wear and tear, potential overtime liability, and municipal administrative fee transparency.
controversies.status: Governed by municipal ordinance; ongoing review of fee structures.

controversies.title: Outside Commercial Holdings & Dual-Role Monitoring
controversies.entityInvolved: Mayor Raymond Grabowski, Councilman Joseph Kolodziej
controversies.summary: Key officials maintain outside private businesses or dual public sector employment while casting votes on municipal policy.
controversies.investigationDetails: Mayor Grabowski operates a private landscaping company and a private investigation/security consulting practice. Councilman Kolodziej serves as the full-time Chief Financial Officer of Mt. Olive Township while holding elected office in Clifton. Under the Local Government Ethics Law, both must maintain rigorous recusals on any municipal contract, zoning change, code enforcement matter, or interlocal agreement that intersects with their private clients or secondary public employer.
controversies.taxpayerImpact: Risk of potential conflicts of interest or perceived favoritism in city inspections, contracts, and vendor selection.
controversies.status: Disclosed on annual FDS at fds.nj.gov; requires active citizen recusal monitoring.
